title: The Resting Membrane and Passive Signals

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Codex accuracy gate → fixes

cards.front: In the lesson's made-up two-leak cell, with the pump's direct current set aside, neither Na+ nor K+ is at equilibrium and each carries a steady current. Why does the membrane potential not move?
cards.back: The outward K+ current and the inward Na+ current are equal and opposite (about 200 pA each), so the net current is zero even though neither ion is at equilibrium.
cards.why: Rest means zero net current, not zero current for each ion.
cards.quote: That is what rest means: zero net current, not zero current for each ion.
cards.section: The standoff

cards.front: What is an ion's equilibrium potential, E_ion?
cards.back: The voltage at which the electrical force on the ion balances its concentration gradient, so the ion feels no net push.
cards.quote: Each ion has an equilibrium potential, E_ion, the voltage at which the electrical force on the ion balances its concentration gradient.
cards.section: The standoff

cards.front: The driving force on an ion is {{c1::Vm − E_ion}}; its size says how hard the ion is pushed and its sign gives the direction.
cards.back: Vm is inside minus outside.
cards.quote: The driving force on an ion is the gap between the marker and that ion's own mark: Vm − E_ion.
cards.section: The standoff

cards.front: For open channels that behave like a resistor (ohmic), the ionic current is I_ion = {{c1::g_ion × (Vm − E_ion)}}, with outward current positive.
cards.back: g is the conductance, mostly how many channels are open; nS × mV gives pA. A positive driving force on a cation gives outward current: the ion leaves.
cards.quote: If that ion's channels are open and behave like a resistor (ohmic), the rope's pull is the ion's current: I_ion = g_ion × (Vm − E_ion)
cards.section: The standoff

cards.front: A neuron sits at −60 mV. E_Na = +55 mV, and its ohmic Na+ leak conductance is 2 nS. What is the Na+ current (outward positive), and which way do Na+ ions move?
cards.back: Driving force = Vm − E_Na = −60 − 55 = −115 mV. I_Na = 2 nS × (−115 mV) = −230 pA: an inward current, so Na+ enters.
cards.quote: By convention, outward current (positive charge leaving) is positive and inward current negative, so a positive driving force on a cation gives outward current: the ion leaves.
cards.section: The standoff

cards.front: Which way does each open channel pull the membrane potential, and what makes the pull stronger?
cards.back: Toward its own reversal potential (for a one-ion channel, that ion's equilibrium potential). The pull is stronger with more conductance and with Vm farther from that potential.
cards.quote: Each open channel pulls the voltage toward its own reversal potential (for a channel that passes one ion, that ion's equilibrium potential), harder the more conductance it has
cards.section: The standoff

cards.front: Where does the membrane voltage head when several leak channels are open, no current is injected and the pump's direct current is set aside?
cards.back: To the balance point, where the pulls cancel and net current is zero: the average of the reversal potentials weighted by their conductances. That balance point is the resting potential.
cards.quote: The voltage heads for the balance point, where the pulls cancel and the net current is zero:
cards.section: The standoff

cards.front: With two ohmic leaks, no injected current and the pump's direct current set aside, the balance point is Vm = {{c1::(g_K E_K + g_Na E_Na) / (g_K + g_Na)}}.
cards.back: Set g_K (Vm − E_K) + g_Na (Vm − E_Na) = 0 and solve for Vm. More ions add more terms above and below the line.
cards.quote: Vm = (g_K E_K + g_Na E_Na) / (g_K + g_Na)
cards.section: Where the leaks balance

cards.front: A neuron has two ohmic leaks: g_K = 9 nS with E_K = −90 mV, and g_Na = 1 nS with E_Na = +60 mV. Where is its resting potential (pump current set aside)?
cards.back: Vm = (9 × −90 + 1 × 60) / (9 + 1) = (−810 + 60) / 10 = −75 mV, near E_K because potassium's conductance is nine times sodium's.
cards.quote: In algebra, set the currents to sum to zero and solve for Vm:
cards.section: Where the leaks balance

cards.front: If more of one ion's leak channels open, which way does the balance point move? If some close?
cards.back: Opening moves it toward that ion's equilibrium potential; closing moves it away.
cards.why: That ion gets more (or less) weight in the conductance-weighted average.
cards.quote: Open more of one ion's channels and the balance point slides toward that ion's equilibrium potential.
cards.section: Where the leaks balance

cards.front: In a compact, isopotential passive neuron with fixed ohmic leaks, every leak conductance is doubled in proportion, with capacitance unchanged. What happens to the passive balance point, the input resistance and the time constant?
cards.back: The balance point does not move, but Rin halves and τ halves.
cards.why: The weights keep the same ratio, so the weighted average is unchanged; Rin = 1/g_total and τ = Rin × C both fall with total conductance.
cards.quote: Scale every leak up or down together and the balance point does not move, though Rin and τ do
cards.section: Where the leaks balance

cards.front: A neuron has ohmic leaks g_K = 9 nS (E_K = −90 mV) and g_Na = 1 nS (E_Na = +60 mV), resting at −75 mV. A drug doubles g_Na to 2 nS. Where is the new rest?
cards.back: Vm = (9 × −90 + 2 × 60) / 11 = −690 / 11 ≈ −62.7 mV. Rest depolarizes toward E_Na, but only partway: potassium still has the larger conductance, so rest stays nearer E_K.
cards.quote: Rest depolarizes toward E_Na, but only partway: potassium's rope is still about 2.8 times stronger, so the marker stays nearer E_K.
cards.section: Where the leaks balance

cards.front: Use the GHK voltage equation with RT/F = 26.72 mV, PK = 1, PNa = 0.04, PCl = 0, [K+] 140 mM in, [Na+] 15 mM in and 145 mM out. External K+ is raised from 4 to 10 mM. What is the new Vm?
cards.quote: Read it as the balance point again: each ion counts in proportion to its permeability, and the equation does the weighting for you.
cards.section: The calculating tool: the GHK equation

cards.front: How does an ion's permeability differ from its conductance?
cards.back: Permeability is a property of the pathway: how easily the ion gets through. Conductance is the current carried per millivolt of driving force, which also depends on the ion concentrations on each side and on the voltage.
cards.quote: Permeability is a property of the pathway: how easily an ion gets through.
cards.section: The calculating tool: the GHK equation

cards.front: In the lesson's model cell, doubling PNa in the GHK equation moves rest to −58.9 mV, but doubling g_Na in the ohmic average gives −53.7 mV. Why does the GHK change shift rest less?
cards.back: GHK leaks are not ohmic: their conductances shift with voltage. Doubling PNa raises g_Na only about 1.9 times and also raises g_K about 1.14 times, so sodium gains less ground.
cards.why: Recomputing the chord conductances at the new rest and putting them in the weighted average returns −58.9 mV.
cards.quote: Doubling PNa raises gNa only about 1.9 times and also raises gK about 1.14 times, so sodium gains less ground
cards.section: The calculating tool: the GHK equation

cards.front: Per ATP, the Na+/K+ pump moves {{c1::three Na+ out and two K+ in}}.
cards.back: It restores the gradients that the leaks run down.
cards.quote: The Na+/K+ pump (three Na+ out, two K+ in per ATP) puts the ions back.
cards.section: What keeps the balance point there: the pump

cards.front: Why is the resting potential a steady state rather than an equilibrium?
cards.back: Leak currents flow all the time and would run the gradients down. The Na+/K+ pump keeps putting the ions back, so rest is held by ongoing pumping.
cards.quote: So rest is a steady state, kept up by the pump, not an equilibrium.
cards.section: What keeps the balance point there: the pump

cards.front: Besides keeping the gradients, what direct effect does the Na+/K+ pump have on the resting potential?
cards.back: It moves net charge outward, a small outward current that shifts real rest somewhat more negative. The size is small in many cells but varies with cell type and pump activity.
cards.quote: it shifts real rest somewhat more negative, by an amount small in many cells but varying with cell type and pump activity.
cards.section: What keeps the balance point there: the pump

cards.front: A small current step is injected into a passive neuron in current clamp. Why does the voltage not jump instantly to its new level?
cards.back: The membrane stores charge, and moving charge takes time. The voltage moves at once but smoothly, steeply at first and then bending toward a plateau.
cards.why: The bilayer is a thin insulator between two conducting solutions, a capacitor in parallel with the leak resistors.
cards.quote: The reason is that the membrane stores charge, and moving charge takes time.
cards.section: A nudge takes time: the RC membrane

cards.front: Membrane capacitance, C, is {{c1::the charge stored per volt}}.
cards.quote: Capacitance, C, is the charge stored per volt.
cards.section: A nudge takes time: the RC membrane

cards.front: In a compact cell with ohmic leaks, input resistance is Rin = ΔV / I = {{c1::1 / g_total}}.
cards.back: ΔV is the steady voltage change produced by a small steady current I.
cards.quote: Rin = ΔV / I = 1 / g_total
cards.section: A nudge takes time: the RC membrane

cards.front: In a compact passive cell with fixed capacitance and fixed ohmic leaks, after a small current step the membrane time constant τ = Rin × C is the time for the voltage to reach {{c1::63%}} of its final change.
cards.back: 1 − e^−1 = 0.632. It is not the time to finish: 2τ gives 86% and 3τ 95%.
cards.quote: The membrane time constant τ is the time to reach 63% of the final change, since 1 − e^−1 = 0.632.
cards.section: A nudge takes time: the RC membrane

cards.front: A compact passive neuron has 5 nS of total ohmic leak and C = 150 pF. A +50 pA step is injected (positive injected current depolarizes). Find Rin, τ, the final deflection, the deflection at one τ and the initial slope.
cards.back: Rin = 1/5 nS = 200 MΩ. τ = 200 MΩ × 150 pF = 30 ms. Final: 50 pA × 200 MΩ = +10 mV. At 30 ms: 10 × 0.632 ≈ +6.3 mV. Initial slope: I/C = 50 pA / 150 pF ≈ 0.33 mV per ms.
cards.quote: ΔV(t) = I × Rin × (1 − e^(−t/τ)), with τ = Rin × C = C / g_total
cards.section: A nudge takes time: the RC membrane

cards.front: In a compact passive cell with fixed capacitance and fixed ohmic leaks, why do responses to two brief, small current pulses add when they arrive within a few τ, and how does a longer τ change this?
cards.back: In this model the first deflection lingers (37% remains one τ after its input ends) and the responses add exactly, so the second builds on it: temporal summation. A longer τ leaves more of the first response, widening the window for adding.
cards.quote: A longer τ leaves a larger share of the first response when the second arrives, so it widens the window for adding
cards.section: A nudge takes time: the RC membrane

cards.front: In a fixed-conductance passive model, two current pulses add exactly. Using the balance-point rule, explain why two synaptic inputs that each open channels need not add linearly.
cards.back: Each synaptic input opens channels. The extra conductance makes any current shift Vm less (shift = I / g_total), and moving Vm changes each input's driving force. So the summed response need not equal the sum of the separate responses.
cards.quote: a synaptic input opens channels, changing both the conductance and the driving force, so its responses need not add linearly.
cards.section: A nudge takes time: the RC membrane

cards.front: For a uniform, effectively infinite passive cable, the length constant is λ = {{c1::√(rm / ri)}}.
cards.back: rm is membrane resistance and ri core (axial) resistance, each for a unit length of cable. Steady voltage falls as V0 × e^(−x/λ).
cards.quote: V(x) = V0 × e^(−x/λ), with λ = √(rm / ri)
cards.section: A nudge fades with distance: the cable

cards.front: What does one length constant mean physically in a passive cable?
cards.back: Over a stretch of cable one λ long, the resistance along the core equals the resistance out through the membrane wall.
cards.quote: Take a stretch of cable one λ long: the resistance along its core equals the resistance out through its wall over that same stretch.
cards.section: A nudge fades with distance: the cable

cards.front: In a uniform infinite passive cable, the steady deflection one length constant from the source is about {{c1::37%}} of its value at the source.
cards.back: e^−1. At 2λ about 14% remains. λ sets the scale of decay; it is not a cutoff.
cards.quote: At one λ the steady deflection is e^−1, about 37% of its value at the source: smaller, not gone.
cards.section: A nudge fades with distance: the cable

cards.front: With membrane and cytoplasm unchanged, how does a dendrite's length constant scale with its diameter, and why does a wider dendrite carry a passive signal farther?
cards.back: λ grows as the square root of diameter. A wider core is an easier path along the cable relative to leaking out through the wall.
cards.quote: With membrane and cytoplasm unchanged, λ grows as the square root of diameter.
cards.section: A nudge fades with distance: the cable

cards.front: A steady +20 mV deflection is held at one point on a uniform, infinite passive dendrite with λ = 0.2 mm. What is the steady deflection 0.4 mm away?
cards.back: 0.4 mm is 2λ, so V = 20 × e^−2 = 20 × 0.135 ≈ 2.7 mV, about 14% of the start.
cards.section: A nudge fades with distance: the cable

cards.front: A passive cable's membrane is made leakier, with its diameter and cytoplasm unchanged. Where does the point at which the steady signal has fallen to 37% move?
cards.back: Toward the source: λ shrinks, so the signal fades over a shorter distance.
cards.why: Leakier membrane lowers rm, and λ = √(rm / ri).
cards.quote: Make the membrane leakier and watch the 37% point move toward the source; widen the cable and watch it move away.
cards.section: A nudge fades with distance: the cable

cards.front: From a single small current step in a compact passive cell, which three numbers can you read, and how?
cards.back: Rin = plateau ΔV / I. τ = time to reach 63% of the plateau. C = τ / Rin.
cards.quote: one current step gives three numbers: Rin = ΔV / I (the plateau divided by the current), τ (the time to 63%), and C = τ / Rin
cards.section: Reading a trace and predicting a drug

cards.front: In a made-up current-clamp recording of a compact passive neuron, a −20 pA step gives a steady −4 mV deflection and reaches 63% of it at 30 ms. Find Rin and C.
cards.back: Rin = 4 mV / 20 pA = 200 MΩ. τ = 30 ms. C = τ / Rin = 30 ms / 200 MΩ = 150 pF.
cards.quote: Small hyperpolarizing steps, which stay away from threshold, plotted as steady ΔV against I give Rin as the slope.
cards.section: Reading a trace and predicting a drug

cards.front: Why does C = τ / Rin underestimate total capacitance in a neuron with substantial dendrites?
cards.back: A steady current at the soma spreads only partway into the dendrites, so Rin is higher than if the whole membrane sat at one voltage, and τ / Rin comes out too small.
cards.quote: In a cell with substantial dendrites, a steady current at the soma spreads only partway into the dendrites
cards.section: Reading a trace and predicting a drug

cards.front: Small hyperpolarizing steps give a straight line of steady ΔV against I. Does that prove the membrane is passive?
cards.back: No. It shows Rin is constant over that range, which fits a passive membrane but does not prove it.
cards.quote: A straight line means Rin is constant over that range, which fits a passive membrane but does not prove it.
cards.section: Reading a trace and predicting a drug

cards.front: During a hyperpolarizing current step, the voltage overshoots and then sags back instead of rising smoothly to a plateau. What does this show, and can a single RC fit be trusted?
cards.back: A conductance is turning on with voltage, often the HCN current, which hyperpolarization switches on. A single RC fit will mislead.
cards.quote: If the voltage overshoots and sags back during a hyperpolarizing step, a conductance is turning on with voltage, often the HCN current, which hyperpolarization switches on.
cards.section: Reading a trace and predicting a drug

cards.front: To predict what a drug does to a passive neuron, which two questions do you ask, and what does each one decide?
cards.back: Which ion's conductance changed, and which way? That moves rest. Did the total conductance go up or down? That moves Rin and τ.
cards.quote: Which ion's conductance changed, and which way? That moves rest. Did the total conductance go up or down? That moves Rin and τ.
cards.section: Reading a trace and predicting a drug

cards.front: A drug opens more Na+ leak channels in a neuron and does nothing else. Predict the change in resting potential, Rin and τ.
cards.back: Rest depolarizes toward E_Na. Total conductance rises, so Rin falls and τ = Rin × C shortens.
cards.quote: More Na+ conductance depolarizes toward ENa and also lowers Rin.
cards.section: Reading a trace and predicting a drug

cards.front: Channels open whose reversal potential equals the resting potential. Why does rest not move?
cards.back: The driving force on them is zero, so they add no net current and no pull on Vm.
cards.why: In the rope picture, the new rope is anchored exactly where the marker already sits.
cards.quote: It is not stretched, so it adds no pull, and rest does not move.
cards.section: Shunting: more conductance, same rest

cards.front: In a neuron where E_Cl equals rest, a small depolarizing current step gives +6 mV. Many chloride channels then open, and the same step is repeated. Predict rest and the response.
cards.back: Rest stays put, but the step now gives less than +6 mV, and the response is faster. This is shunting.
cards.why: g_total is larger, and the shift is I / g_total; τ = C / g_total shortens.
cards.quote: Any other current now shifts the voltage less, because g_total is larger and the shift is I / g_total, and the response is faster too.
cards.section: Shunting: more conductance, same rest

cards.front: Shunting chloride channels open in a passive neuron (E_Cl equal to rest). Predict the effect on temporal summation of two small inputs arriving 15 ms apart.
cards.back: Summation weakens: each response is smaller and the first decays faster, so less of it remains when the second arrives.
cards.why: Added conductance lowers Rin (smaller shift, I / g_total) and shortens τ = Rin × C, narrowing the window for adding.
cards.quote: This is shunting: a conductance that reverses at rest lowers Rin without moving Vm.
cards.section: Shunting: more conductance, same rest

cards.front: In a made-up recording of an isopotential passive neuron (fixed ohmic leaks, fixed specific capacitance), a −40 pA step gives −4 mV with τ = 15 ms. A drug that changes one leak hyperpolarizes rest by 5 mV; the step now gives −2 mV with τ = 7.5 ms. What did the drug do?
cards.back: Rin 100 → 50 MΩ; C = 15/100 = 7.5/50 = 150 pF, unchanged. Total leak 10 → 20 nS, so 10 nS was opened. Opening moves rest toward the reversal potential, so it reversed below rest: −5 mV × 20/10 = 10 mV below. A K+ leak is the likely candidate.
cards.quote: Capacitance did not change, consistent with unchanged membrane area under fixed specific capacitance; τ rose only because Rin did.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A drug is thought to close a K+ leak conductance. What voltage-clamp result would support that reading?
cards.back: Subtract currents with and without the drug at several voltages. A K+ leak gives a drug-sensitive current that reverses near E_K, shifts its reversal when external K+ is raised, and appears without delay after each voltage step.
cards.quote: A K+ leak should give a drug-sensitive current that reverses near EK, shifts its reversal when external K+ is raised, and appears without delay after each voltage step.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A drug opens K+ leak channels uniformly over a neuron's soma and dendrites, with capacitance, geometry and cytoplasm unchanged. Predict rest, Rin, τ, λ, and what happens to a small distal dendritic current input seen at the soma.
cards.back: Rest moves toward E_K. Rin falls, the membrane τ shortens and λ shrinks, because λ = √(rm / ri) and rm drops. The distal input is smaller at the soma, more local, decays faster, and sums less with other inputs. The somatic transient can contain several exponentials; Rin = 1/g_total and τ = Rin × C are for a compact cell.
cards.why: Balance-point rule for rest; cable rule λ = √(rm / ri); a shorter τ narrows the window for temporal summation.
cards.quote: In short: rest is where the leaks balance, and the leak (with capacitance, and in a dendrite the core) decides how big, how fast and how far a nudge goes.
cards.section: The standoff

cards.front: Two compact passive neurons have the same leak conductance and capacitance per unit membrane area, but one has twice the membrane area. Compare their Rin and τ.
cards.back: The larger cell has half the Rin, but the same τ.
cards.why: Doubling area doubles both g_total and C. Rin = 1/g_total halves, while τ = C / g_total is unchanged.
cards.quote: The balance point moves the instant the current starts. The voltage follows it, at a pace set by capacitance and leak:
cards.section: A nudge takes time: the RC membrane
